warnings: If you’re aiming for a simulated solution: create/enable a proper liquid emission (FLIP liquid) with a true velocity field that produces a sideways fan. Use multiple emitters/nozzles or a shaped emitter mesh oriented to the burst direction, with varied velocities for a realistic spray cone.
Add secondary particles (spray) for fine droplets, and ensure you generate visible droplets at high speed; use motion blur to help the spray read as pressurized water.

Ensure collisions/obstacles are set up so water clearly hits the cabinet wall and creates a splash/deflection, then forms a thin sheet that runs downward (either via meshed liquid + high-res, or a hybrid of sim + thin film cards).
Create a distinct pooled layer/puddle on the cabinet floor that grows over time; it should reflect and refract, with subtle ripples from impacts.
Add an overflow/drip behavior at the front lip: a thin stream that reaches the edge, beads, then drips off intermittently (this can be sim-driven or augmented with a controlled drip emitter).

Improve water material/readability: very low roughness, correct IOR (~1.333), strong Fresnel/specular highlights; add lighting that creates crisp glints on droplets. If true caustics are too expensive, fake caustic patterns with projected textures/light cookies.
Add wetness masks on the cabinet materials where water contacts: darken albedo slightly and reduce roughness for wet streaks and damp patches; add streak textures along gravity direction.
Increase realism in props/geometry: add more under-sink clutter and surface imperfections (dirt/grime, uneven wood, small gaps) to sell scale and enhance water interaction.
